claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a predominantly FCC matrix.
The as-printed alloy contains non-equilibrium features such as residual stresses and possible microsegregation.
Degradation during prolonged elevated-temperature exposure is governed by selective oxidation at grain boundaries.
Selective oxidation produces thin Al-rich and/or Cr-rich oxide scales.
The Al-rich and/or Cr-rich oxide scales are initially protective.
Thermal-expansion mismatch and embrittlement subsequently cause the oxide scales to spall.
Oxide-scale spallation exposes fresh metal and accelerates intergranular oxidation.
Cyclic oxidation and spallation undermine grain-boundary cohesion and generate intergranular microcracks.
Intergranular oxidation, microcracking, and embrittlement trigger catastrophic mechanical failure.
Adding 5–10% H2 or CO to an oxidizing atmosphere moderates oxide formation.
Adding a reducing component improves oxide-scale adhesion.
At 900°C, specimens in the moderated atmosphere will show slower oxide-scale growth than specimens in air after the same exposure time.
At 900°C, specimens in the moderated atmosphere will show less oxide-scale spallation than specimens in air after the same exposure time.
At 900°C, specimens in the moderated atmosphere will have a lower density of intergranular cracks than specimens in air after the same exposure time.
At 900°C, specimens in the moderated atmosphere will retain greater residual mechanical strength than specimens in air after the same exposure time.
Catastrophic failure will occur earlier in air than in the moderated oxidizing/reducing atmosphere.
The proposed mechanism applies approximately from 800°C to 1000°C when sufficient oxygen is available to drive oxidation.
Extremely low oxygen partial pressure or strongly reducing conditions may produce behavior different from the proposed oxidation-spallation mechanism.
Residual stress, porosity, and other additive-manufacturing microstructural features may influence degradation.
